newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aborigines say land at core of racial tensions.
newsitem.headline: Aborigines say land at core of racial tensions.

text.p: A major Aboriginal conference held to mend black-white relations in Australia ended on Wednesday warning that racial harmony could not be achieved without an end to the nation's 200-year-old land conflict.

Aboriginal leaders also called for a government apology and compensation to the tens of thousands of Aborigines taken from parents under an assimilation policy labelled genocidal by Australia's Human Rights Commission.

But Prime Minister John Howard stood firm and refused to issue a government apology or compensation, despite an emotional parliamentary debate which saw the Labor opposition leader cry when he apologised to Aborigines for past ill-treatment.

Many of the 2,000 mostly Aboriginal delegates at the Aboriginal Reconciliation Convention painted Howard as a villain and described him as a major obstacle to the goal of achieving racial reconciliation by the centenary of nationhood in 2001.
"I don't think we in Australia have the leadership to take us to reconciliation in 2001," said Noel Pearson, legal adviser to the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission.
"There is a pressing need for a moral or philosophical lobotomy or heart transplant on the part of our national leadership," Pearson added.

The three-day convention, held as a first step toward drafting a form of reconciliation treaty by year 2000, headed its resolutions with a call for Howard to respect a recent court decision enabling Aborigines to share land with farmers.
"Without co-existence there can be no reconciliation," Rick Farley, a former lobbyist for the pastoral industry and a member of the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation, told delegates.
"The simple reality is that land is absolutely essential to Aboriginal lore and culture, so while there is an Aboriginal culture there will be a land agenda."
Since white settlement in 1788, land has been at the heart of conflict, much of it bloody. First settlers shot and poisoned Aborigines. Aborigines burnt homesteads and murdered settlers.
Aborigines only won native land title in 1993 but Howard has warned that up to 78 percent of Australia's 7.68 million square km (2.96 million square miles) could ultimately be claimed.
Howard angered Aboriginal delegates on Monday in a lectern-thumping speech defending his new plan to limit native title on farm land. Many delegates turned their backs on him.

But Howard did offer a personal apology over the other big issue seen as a threat to reconciliation -- the past government policy of forcibly taking Aboriginal children away from their parents and assimilating them into the white community.
Tens of thousands of Aborigines, dubbed the "Stolen Generation", demand a parliamentary apology and compensation.
In a sign of the gulf separating the government from Aborigines on this issue, Howard confirmed after the conference closed on Wednesday that compensation would not be granted.

"This is asking one generation to accept legal responsibility for the acts of earlier generations. Once a nation begins to go down that path, there is in fact no end," Howard told parliament in Canberra.
Aboriginal leader Pat Dodson, chairman of the official Council for Aboriginal Reconcilation, said he doubted Howard's word was final, saying parliament would decide the issue.
The conference's many recommendations also included constitutional changes to protect native languages and culture. It also mooted reserved parliamentary seats for Aborigines.
Unlike the U.S. constitution, Australia's constitution sets out government rights, not individual rights.
Aborigines make up two percent of Australia's 18 million population, but not one Aborigine sits in national parliament.
